idiom_name: std::async/std::future accumulation, std::latch (C++20) or condition_variable collector
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the pieces but not the pattern: std::async returns a std::future per sub-request, std::latch/std::barrier (C++20) or a std::condition_variable plus std::mutex implement the count-based completeness condition, and the merge is a hand-written collector because there is no std::when_all before C++26. Prefer the futures form when the aggregator itself spawns the work (pull style: collect the futures and get() them), and the latch/condition-variable form when partial messages are pushed in by the transport, where a completion callback is invoked once the count or deadline is reached. The classic stateful collector stays justified exactly in the push case and whenever de-duplication, expiry and correlation bookkeeping are required, since none of the stdlib primitives understand message identity.
pitfalls: A discarded std::async(std::launch::async) future blocks in its destructor until the task finishes (and a deferred one may never run): keep the futures in a container and get() them.
std::latch signals completion but does not protect the partial-result container - merging into a shared vector still needs a mutex or a single owning thread.
Exception propagation: f.get() rethrows the task's exception, so one failed ask abandons the remaining results unless each future is guarded with try/catch or a packaged_task wrapper.
